client: I've been really struggling with my new job lately. I'm the only junior marketer on the team, and everyone else seems to know exactly what they're doing while I'm constantly second-guessing myself. I lie awake at night worrying that they'll realize they made a mistake hiring me.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling overwhelmed by the pressure to perform and comparing yourself to your more experienced colleagues—that's a tough spot to be in. What might it look like to challenge the thought that you're a "mistake hire" by focusing on the skills and qualities that got you this position in the first place?

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard to believe in my skills when I see how effortlessly everyone else handles things. My boss asked me to present some campaign ideas yesterday, and I completely blanked out - that doesn't exactly scream "qualified hire" to me. It makes me wonder if my resume just made me look better than I actually am.
therapist: It sounds like that moment of blanking out felt really discouraging, and it's easy to fixate on those moments as proof of not being "good enough." What if we explored how you might prepare differently next time to feel more confident, and how you could reframe that experience as a learning opportunity rather than a failure?

client: I know I should probably see it as a learning experience, but in the moment it just felt humiliating. My face got so hot and I could see my boss trying to hide his disappointment. Maybe I could prepare more next time, but what if I freeze up again no matter what? That fear makes me want to avoid presenting altogether.
therapist: That fear of freezing again sounds so intense, and I can hear how that moment of embarrassment is still weighing heavily on you. What would it feel like to acknowledge that even experienced professionals have moments where they blank out, and that this doesn't define your overall competence?

client: I guess I know logically that everyone makes mistakes, but it feels different when it's me. I keep replaying that moment in my head, and it makes me feel like I'm not cut out for this role. Even if other people mess up sometimes, I feel like I'm just not as naturally talented as they are, and that's harder to fix.
therapist: It seems like you're holding yourself to a much higher standard than you would for others, which can make even small mistakes feel like proof of inadequacy. What might it be like to explore whether "natural talent" is really the most important factor here, or if persistence and learning from experience could be just as valuable?

client: I suppose I do expect myself to be perfect right away, but that's because I feel like I don't have time to learn slowly. Everyone else already seems to have it all figured out. It's hard to believe persistence will be enough when I feel like I'm constantly playing catch-up.
therapist: It sounds like you're putting tremendous pressure on yourself to match your colleagues' experience level immediately, which must feel exhausting. What might happen if you allowed yourself the same grace to learn and grow that your organization clearly did when they hired you as a junior team member?

client: I know logically that I shouldn't compare myself to people with years more experience, but it's hard not to when we're all working on the same projects together. I guess what really scares me is that maybe they expect me to be at their level already, even though I'm technically the junior hire. That pressure makes me feel like I can't admit when I don't know something.
therapist: It makes complete sense that this environment would make you feel extra pressure, especially when you're unsure about the unspoken expectations. How might it feel to reframe asking questions not as showing weakness, but as demonstrating your commitment to getting things right?

client: I never thought about it that way before, but I'm still worried my questions might make me look incompetent. When my coworker asked me something basic last week, I could tell she was surprised I didn't know it, and that really stuck with me. Maybe I'm just overthinking her reaction, but it makes me hesitant to ask anything now.
therapist: That moment with your coworker seems to have left a lasting impression, and it's understandable that it would make you feel hesitant about asking questions now. What might it look like to explore whether her surprise was truly judgmental, or if it could simply have been momentary surprise that didn't reflect her overall opinion of you?

client: You're right that I might be reading too much into her reaction. But even if it wasn't judgmental, the fact that it was something basic makes me worry about all the other gaps in my knowledge. It feels like every time I encounter something I don't know, it's proof I don't belong here.
therapist: It sounds like each moment of not knowing something gets added to a growing list of "proof" against you, which must feel incredibly heavy to carry. What if we explored how you might reframe these gaps not as failures, but simply as the natural learning curve that every professional goes through in a new role?

client: I can see how I might be interpreting gaps in my knowledge too harshly, but it's hard to shake the feeling that I should already know these things. When I see how easily my coworkers handle tasks, it makes me feel like I'm so far behind where I should be, even though I know logically I'm still learning. It's frustrating to feel like I'm always the one who needs help.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between understanding intellectually that learning takes time, and this visceral feeling of being behind that's hard to ignore. What would it be like to notice when you're making these comparisons, and gently remind yourself that your coworkers likely had moments like this too—they're just not visible to you now?

client: That makes sense in theory, but when I'm actually in the office seeing how smoothly everything runs when I'm not involved, it's hard to believe they ever struggled like I am. I keep thinking - if they did have rough starts, why don't they ever talk about it? It makes me feel like my struggles are abnormal or something to be ashamed of.
therapist: It seems like the lack of visible struggle from your colleagues makes your own challenges feel isolating and even more difficult to accept. What if we considered that people often don't share their early struggles precisely because of this same fear—that it might make them look incompetent or vulnerable?
